citeAs: Pan, J., Wang, X., Neubig, G., Jaitly, N., Ji, H., Suhr, A., Zhang, Y. (2025). Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym. Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267.
creator: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang (UC Berkeley, UIUC, CMU, Apple)
description: SWE-Gym is the first environment for training software engineering (SWE) agents, containing 2,438 real-world task instances sourced from pull requests in 11 popular Python repositories. Each instance comprises a Python codebase with an executable runtime environment, pre-installed dependencies, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language derived from GitHub issues. It is designed to support training of language model-based SWE agents and verifier models.
name: SWE-Gym
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotations were done by a subset of the authors (researchers from UC Berkeley, UIUC, CMU, and Apple). No further demographic details are provided.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Manual annotation by authors; OpenHands remote runtime was used to parallelize execution of agent trajectories and unit tests.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations (environment setup and validation) were performed by a subset of the authors. Dependencies for each task instance were manually configured using relevant configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script was used to verify that the gold patch passes more unit tests than the original code.
rai:dataBiases: Task distribution across repositories exhibits a long-tail pattern: tasks associated with pandas comprise nearly one-third of the total, whereas tasks related to bokeh represent only about one percent. The authors note that ignoring executable environment configuration could introduce distribution bias. Repeated sampling shows that task success probability follows a long-tail distribution biased toward easier tasks, which can negatively impact training if not addressed (mitigated via per-instance capping). The dataset focuses exclusively on Python repositories, limiting language diversity.
rai:dataCollection: Repositories were identified using SEART GitHub search, filtering for Python repositories created before July 1, 2022 with more than 500 stars, at least 300 lines of code, more than 500 pull requests, and 100 contributors, resulting in 358 repositories. SWE-Bench's instance extraction script was used to convert repositories into task instances, each corresponding to a GitHub issue including the natural language description, a snapshot of the repository, and a set of unit tests. Executable environments were manually configured using relevant configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script was used to ensure that the gold patch passes more unit tests than the original code. The process required approximately 200 human annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of Python GitHub repositories and their associated pull requests and issues. Over 358 repositories, 64,689 task instances were extracted (referred to as SWE-Gym Raw), each containing code, issue descriptions, and solutions but without executable environments or guaranteed unit test effectiveness.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Repositories created before July 1, 2022 were selected; the exact end date of data collection is not specified beyond this cutoff.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataLimitations: SWE-Gym is limited by its environment diversity, including the number of repositories (11 with executable environments), types of tasks, and programming languages (Python only). The dataset focuses on repository-level software engineering tasks from GitHub issues and may not generalize to other software engineering scenarios. The authors note that automatic environment synthesis, broader repository coverage, and support for additional programming languages are important future directions.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: A subset of 230 tasks (SWE-Gym Lite) was identified following the SWE-Bench Lite filtering pipeline, excluding tasks requiring editing more than one file, tasks with poorly described problem statements, those with excessively complex ground-truth code diffs, and tests focused on error message validation. Per-instance capping was introduced to limit the maximum number of selected samples per task to mitigate bias toward easier tasks in training data.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Instances were filtered using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure the gold patch passes more unit tests than the original code. Version training instances were associated with version numbers and environments were set up version-by-version. Dependencies were manually configured for each task instance. Failed instances were filtered out, resulting in 2,438 validated instances from 11 repositories. Pre-built Docker images were created for each instance for full reproducibility (totaling 6 TB).
rai:dataSocialImpact: Improving automated software engineering capabilities could increase developer productivity and accessibility across industries. As agents become more capable, they may impact software engineering jobs and require careful consideration around code ownership, licensing, and attribution. Similar techniques could potentially be misused to automate the creation of malicious code. The authors encourage future work to explore frameworks for responsible deployment, including considerations around security, safety, and economic impacts.
rai:dataUseCases: Training language model-based software engineering agents via supervised fine-tuning and rejection sampling. Training verifier (outcome-supervised reward) models for inference-time scaling. Benchmarking and evaluating SWE agent performance. Research into self-improvement of LM agents for software engineering tasks. Studying training-time and inference-time scaling behaviors for SWE agents.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SWE-Bench's instance extraction script and execution-based validation script were used for instance extraction and validation. SEART GitHub search was used for repository filtering. The Qwen-2.5-Coder-Instruct tokenizer (7B) was used to estimate token counts in trajectory statistics. GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) and Claude (claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022) were used to sample agent trajectories for training data collection.

null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: No inter-annotator agreement metrics or formal annotation quality analysis described; validation is done via automated unit test execution.
null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: No specific number of independent annotations per item is described; environment setup was done once per instance.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not explicitly discuss missing data handling beyond filtering out failed instances during validation.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol described; failed instances are filtered out rather than imputed.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan described beyond the initial public release.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Dataset consists of GitHub issues and code repositories; no personal or sensitive information is discussed.
